title: Malcolm X at Hajj
hookLine: he writes home from Mecca of pilgrims of every color in one brotherhood

lines: THE SAME PLATE, THE SAME FLOOR.
cards: A tall American in two plain white cloths, the pilgrim's dress, sits down to write a letter home. For years he has been the fiery voice of a movement in America, speaking hard words about race.
Now he is in Mecca, and something in him is shifting. He has walked around the Ka'ba in a crowd from every part of the world.
He has eaten from the same plate and slept on the same floor as men whose skin, he writes, ranged from the palest to the darkest. He says he has never seen anything like it. Today: Malcolm X at Hajj.

teach.b: The man was Malcolm X, and his autobiography gives a chapter to the pilgrimage and the letters he wrote from it.
He describes praying, eating and sleeping beside pilgrims of every color, and says the experience made him rethink much of what he had believed about race.

teach.h: A NEW NAME: EL-HAJJ MALIK EL-SHABAZZ.
teach.b: He went home with a new name, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, and a new way of talking about people. What did he see? The Hajj doing what it is built to do.

teach.h: THE SAME CLOTH, THE SAME HOUSE.
teach.b: Every pilgrim wears the same simple cloth. Every pilgrim faces the same House. In the rows of prayer, a rich man stands by a poor one and a king could stand by a farmer, heel to heel and shoulder to shoulder.
The Qur'an sets human difference beside the sky and the earth: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours."

teach.h: LANGUAGES AND COLORS, AMONG HIS SIGNS.
teach.b: Colors and languages as signs to wonder at, not ranks to climb.

A saying reported from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in his farewell sermon makes a similar point: no Arab over a non-Arab, and no one of one color over another, except by mindfulness of God.
Malcolm did not live long after.
But the letter stayed, and so did the picture: every color, one row.

how: Pilgrims on Hajj wear the same simple white garments, pray in shared rows and travel the same route together, and many Muslims speak of the pilgrimage as a lesson in the equality of believers.

o: any visit to a mosque outside the prayer times
the fast kept during the month of Ramadan
the pilgrimage to Mecca, all in the same plain cloth

games.q: Malcolm X at Hajj — tap the pairs.
p: the name he took after Hajj
no color over another, but by mindfulness of God

s: Malcolm X wrote letters home from Mecca
in his autobiography, the letters describe pilgrims of every color.
the Qur'an treats differences of color as a mark of rank
Qur'an 30:22 counts the difference of languages and colors among God's signs.

games.q: you're on Hajj, at the long meal after the day's rites. the man beside you speaks no language you know. what do you do?
o: eat in silence and move on.
games.why: Malcolm X wrote of eating from the same plate and sleeping on the same floor as pilgrims from everywhere.

practice: Bring to mind a time you stood side by side with people very different from you, at a stadium, a funeral, a kitchen in a crisis, a prayer hall, and what made the differences go quiet for a while.
Then picture one person who seems other to you, by color, country, accent or faith, on your right, shoulder to shoulder, facing the same way. If you pray, ask God's blessing on them.

wordCard.voice: Hajj, the pilgrimage that sent Malcolm X home with a new name after praying beside pilgrims of every color. Today's word, and the end of a week that went from the caliphate's end and partition to Britain and America.

carryVoice: Your line: every color, one row. Difference is a sign to wonder at. Same time tomorrow.
